name: Spiti, locally Piti
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Sharma, Suhnu R. 1979. Phonological structure of Spiti. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 4(2): 83-110. (open scan: SEALang SALA archive,https://sealang.net/sala/archives/pdf8/sharma1979phonological.pdf)
catalog_locator: p. 83 (introduction, last paragraph) and p. 104 (section 'Supra-segmentals', pp. 104-110; duration remark p. 105)
catalog_quote: The present study is the first linguistic work on the spoken language of Spiti and deals with the phonetic and phonemic structure of the segmental and suprasegmental sounds. Among the segmentals seven vowels and thirty-one consonants have been established. Three tones, three pitch-levels of intonational phonemes, three terminal contours, three junctures, and nazalization are found among suprasegmentals. [p. 83] ... Supra-segmentals: A three term tonal system, falling, level and rising tone is found in Spiti and associated with the word or lexical item. A given lexical item may be assigned to one or the other supra-segmental category and termed as a Tone 1 word, a Tone 2 word, or a Tone 3 word (henceforth these tones will be referred to by their descriptive names as Tone 1, falling tone; Tone 2, level tone, and Tone 3, rising tone. [p. 104] ... The syllable bearing falling tone is longer in duration than one bearing the rising tone or the level tone. [p. 105]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (28-page scan scan, no text; the PDF's metadata: 28 pp, 432x588 pt) via the saved scanned (per-page the page scan +.pgm) and rendered the page scan p-01 (= journal p. 83) and p-22 (= journal p. 104) to PNG and read them visually. Both quoted passages are on the page scan exactly as reported: p. 83 last paragraph 'Three tones, three pitch-levels of intonational phonemes, three terminal contours, three junctures, and nazalization are found among suprasegmentals.' (spelling 'nazalization' is in the print); p. 104 under the heading 'Supra-segmentals': 'A three term tonal system, falling, level and rising tone is found in Spiti and associated with the word or lexical item. A given lexical…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Spiti is described as a lexical tone language: every word belongs to one of three tone classes (Tone 1 falling, Tone 2 level, Tone 3 rising), with phrase-level intonation contours and junctures on top. The suprasegmental inventory is enumerated exhaustively and stress/accent is not among its members; no source examined states a stress position. The later LSI Bhotia sketch (three tones + nasalization), Hein 2017 (register tone) and Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 (two-way high/low pitch tone for the W section incl. Spiti) agree that the word-level prosodic contrast is tonal.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Sharma 1979 notes falling-tone syllables are longer than level/rising ones (p. 105); LSI 2023 notes falling tone does not occur word-initially (p. 1034); Mehta 2021 found only five tone-bearing words in her Pin-valley data (p. 112).
new_statements.domain_note: Word/lexical-item level tone assignment (Sharma 1979 p. 104: 'associated with the word or lexical item'); intonational pitch levels and terminal contours are utterance-level (pp. 107-110). Sharma's data: Spiti valley fieldwork 1972-73, 'the whole valley'.
new_statements.identity_note: Sharma 1979 describes 'Spiti (locally Piti)' from valley-wide fieldwork 1972-73 = spit1240. Hein 2001/2017 describe the Tabo village variety (Tabo Tibetan, 'as identical to Spiti Tibetan' per Hein 2017: 113) = spit1240. The LSI 2023 'Bhotia' chapter is Himachal Bhotia recorded in Spiti with informants also from Kullu/Manali (winter migrants) = Spiti Bhoti, possibly with Lahaul (Stod Bhoti, stod1241) admixture. Mehta 2021's consultant is from Sangnam, Pin valley (Spiti). Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 treat Spiti with Garzha and Khunu-Töt as the Western section.

tone_statements.citation: Kato, Atsushi. 2001. [Study of the Spiti dialect; cited as Kato (2001) by Tournadre & Suzuki 2023: 606 among the few descriptions devoted to Spiti].
tone_statements.quote: There are two tones: /"1thigh tone) and /‑/aow tone). They are word tones, which cover one or two syllables as their domain. This is called "tone domain" in this paper. Tone domain can never cover more than two syllables. Tones are represented by putting /N/ or 1‑/ before the first syllable of the tone domain. When the tone domain covers one syllable, each tone takes pitches as fo11ows: ... 1"1 (high tone) : [44]‑‑[43] /‑/ (low tone): [23]
tone_statements.summary: Two word tones, high [44]~[43] and low [23], over a tone domain of one or two syllables, with toneless ('atonic') syllables after it; one tonal minimal pair found; tentative, unlike Sharma 1979.

tone_statements.citation: Nishi, Yoshio (西 義郎). 1986. Gendai Chibetto-go hōgen no bunrui [A classification of Tibetan dialects] [in Japanese]. Kokuritsu Minzokugaku Hakubutsukan Kenkyū Hōkoku / Bulletin of the National Museum of Ethnology 11(4): 837-900. (issue dated 1987-03-31)
tone_statements.quote: しかし，声調体系は全く別である。Ｓｈａｒｍａは，この方言の声調記述で声調の領域を音節でなく，語であるとし，三つの対立的声調を認めて，それぞれトーン（Ｔｏｎｅ）１／＼／を降調，トーン２／一／を平調，トーン３／／／を昇調と呼んでいる。ただし，音節数その他の条件が異なれば，実際の調値も異なるようである。 ... 起点を取って考えるなら，トーン１は，高調で，トーン２とトーン３は，いずれも低調ということになる。この方言では，母音の短・長や音節の短・長と声調の間に相関的な関係はない。
tone_statements.translation: But the tone system is entirely different [from the Central dialects]. Sharma, in his tone description of this dialect, takes the domain of tone to be not the syllable but the word, recognises three contrastive tones, and calls Tone 1 /\/ falling, Tone 2 /-/ level and Tone 3 /// rising. If the number of syllables or other conditions differ, however, the actual tone values also appear to differ. ... Judged by their starting points, Tone 1 is a high tone and Tones 2 and 3 are both low tones. In this dialect there is no correlation between vowel length or syllable length and tone.
tone_statements.locator: p. 877, §4.1 非中央方言型の声調方言; cf. fn. 24 p. 855 'スピティ方言が声調言語であることは明らかである'
tone_statements.summary: Calls Spiti clearly a tone language unlike Central Tibetan; after Sharma 1979: three contrastive tones with the word as domain, falling (high onset), level and rising (low onset); no tie to length.

tone_statements.quote: The Spiti dialect is a form of Central Tibetan. ... In the most characteristic feature, however, viz., in the use of tones, it marches with Central Tibetan. ... Such words are pronounced in the deep tone. ... Tones and accents are the same as in the Central Dialect. The difference between low-toned aspirates derived from old uncompound soft consonants and high-toned aspirates derived from old soft consonants with a prefix, is more marked than in other dialects.

tone_statements.summary: Tones as in Central Tibetan: old plain voiced initials (now aspirated) and old z/zh give the deep (low) tone, old voiced initials with a prefix the high tone; no count or further detail given here.
